messages.story.cover.title: The Garden Is Waiting

messages.story.scene.01.title: At the edge of Menet
messages.story.scene.01.caption: I rest beneath the hills and the wide French sky.
messages.story.scene.01.narration: [softly] At the edge of Menet, beneath the hills and wide French sky... I wait.
messages.story.scene.02.title: Quiet does not mean empty
messages.story.scene.02.caption: Beneath the soil, roots are searching — and a thousand small lives are waiting.
messages.story.scene.02.narration: [reflective] Quiet is not empty. Beneath my soil, roots search - and a thousand small lives wait.
messages.story.scene.03.title: Sunlight is not enough
messages.story.scene.03.caption: Bare soil loses its water. Lonely plants struggle. Surplus disappears when nothing is shared.
messages.story.scene.03.narration: [concerned] But sunlight is not enough. Bare soil loses water. Lonely plants struggle. What is not shared... disappears.
messages.story.scene.04.title: Then young hands arrived
messages.story.scene.04.caption: Not with a perfect plan, but with questions, seeds — and the courage to begin.
messages.story.scene.04.narration: [with quiet hope] Then young hands arrived. Not with a perfect plan, but with questions, seeds - and courage.
messages.story.scene.05.title: Every part found a purpose
messages.story.scene.05.caption: Rain was caught. Mulch cooled the soil. Flowers offered pollinators food. Yesterday’s waste became tomorrow’s growth.
messages.story.scene.05.narration: [warmly] Rain was caught. Mulch cooled the soil. Flowers called pollinators home. Waste became tomorrow's growth.
messages.story.scene.06.title: I became more than a garden
messages.story.scene.06.caption: A web of relationships — between soil and water, wildlife and people, harvest and generosity.
messages.story.scene.06.narration: [with growing wonder] I became a living web: soil and water, wildlife and people, harvest and generosity.
messages.story.scene.07.title: Now I need another pair of eyes
messages.story.scene.07.caption: Yours. Listen closely. Notice what is missing. Help every part find its place — and help me come alive.
messages.story.scene.07.narration: [almost a whisper] Now I need your eyes. Listen. Notice what is missing. Help every part find its place... and help me come alive.
messages.journey.soil.label: Begin with my soil
messages.journey.soil.why: Choose compost or mulch, then place it where the bare ground needs care.
messages.journey.soil.voice: Feed me first. Everything visible begins with the life beneath.
messages.journey.water.label: Catch and keep water
messages.journey.water.why: Add rain harvesting. Later, place a growing area nearby so stored water has somewhere useful to go.
messages.journey.water.voice: Rain should not rush away. Give it somewhere useful to pause.
messages.journey.food.label: Grow food in layers
messages.journey.food.why: Add an edible bed, fruit tree, herb spiral or planted arch. A seed bank can prepare a crop, but the act is complete when food is growing.
messages.journey.food.voice: Let one place feed roots, leaves, fruit — and the people who tend me.
messages.journey.shelter.label: Make a home for wildlife
messages.journey.shelter.why: Plant flowers or add a bug hotel or bird house. A garden is more resilient when it is shared.
messages.journey.shelter.voice: Leave a little room for lives you may never see at first.
messages.journey.share.label: Let one gift circulate
messages.journey.share.why: Pick one glowing cherry cluster and share it from your harvest basket. Or grow a genuine spare before giving an element away.
messages.journey.share.voice: What leaves my gate is not lost. It becomes someone else’s beginning.
messages.journey.challenge.label: Turn to the next season
messages.journey.challenge.why: Advance the season and solve one garden challenge. Your answer will leave a lasting effect.
messages.journey.challenge.voice: Turn the season. Read what changed, then act with the whole system in mind.
messages.journey.complete.label: The garden is ready to reflect
messages.journey.complete.why: You have cared for soil, water, food, habitat, community and a changing season — and connected at least one useful relationship. The ending is now yours to open.
messages.journey.ready.label: Connect what you have built
messages.journey.nudge.share.title: Now give one away
messages.journey.nudge.share.text: Your basket has something to spare — find it beside the community sharing table. Press Share next to it; this act asks for a gift, not a bigger harvest.
messages.journey.nudge.pick.title: Pick the glowing cherries
messages.journey.nudge.pick.text: Tap a glowing cherry cluster on the plot. Your basket then appears beside the community sharing table, ready to give one away.
messages.journey.nudge.grow.title: Grow something worth giving
messages.journey.nudge.grow.text: The garden is asking for a gift. Harvest a crop or pick ripe fruit first, then share one.
messages.journey.nudge.season.title: Turn to the next season
messages.journey.nudge.season.text: Press Next season above the plot. A challenge will meet you there — that is where the garden teaches.
messages.unlock.sharing.title: The community table is open
messages.unlock.sharing.text: Whatever your garden can spare can now go to the table. Giving is not losing here — the shared pool is what carries this place through a bad year.
messages.unlock.seedbank.title: You can sow your own seed now
messages.unlock.seedbank.text: The seed bank is standing. Click it — or the Seed bank button up in the header — to choose what to sow, read what each plant wants, and swap packets with neighbours.
messages.unlock.kitchen.title: You can keep what you grow
messages.unlock.kitchen.text: The garden kitchen is built. Simmer, dry, ferment or simply store — press the Kitchen button in the header and decide how each harvest should last.
messages.unlock.askGarden.title: The garden can be asked now
messages.unlock.askGarden.text: You have made enough for the garden to have something of yours to look at. Press ✦ Ask the garden for help in the right-hand panel — it will read your plot and offer one thing worth trying.
messages.unlock.seedSaved.title: A harvest of your own seed
messages.unlock.seedSaved.text: Some of what you just picked went back into the seed bank. Seed you saved yourself sows for free, ignores the season’s single packet, and can be given away.
messages.catalog.compost.name: Compost
messages.catalog.compost.description: A three-stage bin system that turns kitchen scraps and garden waste into dark, living soil.
messages.catalog.compost.why: It keeps many local organic materials in the nutrient cycle, returning them to the soil instead of treating them as waste. Compost heaps can shelter wildlife, including hedgehogs, so check carefully before turning or forking one.
messages.catalog.hugel.name: Hügelkultur bed
messages.catalog.hugel.description: An experimental raised bed with woody material beneath organic matter, soil and mulch.
messages.catalog.hugel.why: Buried wood may add organic matter and retain some moisture as it decays, but evidence is limited and results vary with climate, soil, construction and time. Monitor settling, moisture and plant growth.
messages.catalog.rain.name: Rain harvesting
messages.catalog.rain.description: A covered, stable barrel or tank that catches water from a suitable roof through a screened inlet.
messages.catalog.rain.why: Stored rain can reduce mains-water use for irrigation. Treat it as non-potable, follow local rules, secure the lid and base, screen mosquitoes and direct overflow safely. A closed barrel is not a wildlife drinking place.
messages.catalog.mulch.name: Mulch / no-dig
messages.catalog.mulch.description: Sheet mulching with cardboard, leaves and wood chips, laid on top instead of digging.
messages.catalog.mulch.why: It slows evaporation, feeds soil organisms and suppresses many weeds; low disturbance helps protect soil structure and fungal networks.
messages.catalog.bugHotel.name: Bug hotel
messages.catalog.bugHotel.description: Stacked wood, hollow canes and bricks full of nooks for insects.
messages.catalog.bugHotel.why: When well designed and kept dry, its varied cavities can offer nesting or overwintering space for some solitary insects.
messages.catalog.arch.name: Growing arch
messages.catalog.arch.description: A vertical structure for climbing plants — beans, peas, cucumbers and small squash.
messages.catalog.arch.why: Vertical growing can make useful growing space above a small footprint and cast a cooler edge nearby, although yield and shade depend on crop, sun, soil and care. Beans and peas also host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules; that relationship feeds the plant first, not the whole bed automatically.
messages.catalog.herbSpiral.name: Herb spiral
messages.catalog.herbSpiral.description: A spiral mound that packs many herbs into one sunny footprint.
messages.catalog.herbSpiral.why: Its height and aspect may create somewhat wetter, drier, sunnier and shadier pockets, but the result depends on soil, rainfall, construction and the site. Observe the pockets rather than assuming every spiral behaves the same.
messages.catalog.pollinator.name: Flower strip
messages.catalog.pollinator.description: A strip of locally suitable flowering plants and perennials along the beds.
messages.catalog.pollinator.why: A long flowering season offers nectar and pollen while bringing pollinators close to crops that benefit from their visits.
messages.catalog.greenhouse.name: Greenhouse
messages.catalog.greenhouse.description: A glass or polytunnel house for raising seedlings and prolonging the season.
messages.catalog.greenhouse.why: It can extend harvests at both ends of the year and buffer some cold, wind and rain. An unheated structure is not frost-proof, so tender crops may still need fleece, a cloche or another suitable protection.
messages.catalog.seedBank.name: Seed bank
messages.catalog.seedBank.description: Labelled, fully dry seed saved from healthy open-pollinated plants and stored for another season.
messages.catalog.seedBank.why: Careful selection over several generations may develop useful local traits. Hybrid seed may not breed true, and isolation distance, population size and the crop’s biology all matter.
messages.catalog.birdBath.name: Bird bath
messages.catalog.birdBath.description: A shallow, regularly cleaned drinking and bathing place for wildlife — separate from crop irrigation.
messages.catalog.birdBath.why: Fresh shallow water with an easy escape route can support birds and insects through dry spells. When birds are using it, replace the water daily and clean the bath at least weekly to reduce disease spread. It does not store enough water for thirsty beds.
messages.catalog.birdHouse.name: Bird house
messages.catalog.birdHouse.description: A nest box for cavity-nesting birds.
messages.catalog.birdHouse.why: A correctly sized, safely placed box may support a suitable cavity-nesting species. It can go up at any time, although autumn is ideal; never disturb an active nest.
messages.catalog.bench.name: Bench
messages.catalog.bench.description: A simple seat tucked among the beds — care for people, not just plants.
messages.catalog.bench.why: A garden you linger in is a garden you tend: rest, observe and share it with the community.
messages.catalog.sign.name: Garden sign
messages.catalog.sign.description: Hand-painted labels naming the plants and beds.
messages.catalog.sign.why: It turns the garden into an open-air classroom for every visitor who walks through.
messages.catalog.appleTree.name: Apple tree
messages.catalog.appleTree.description: A young grafted apple tree from the community swap — planted while dormant, then given years to establish.
messages.catalog.appleTree.why: A fruit tree is the garden’s long game. Most apples need pollen from a different compatible cultivar flowering at the same time, carried by insects. In this training garden, place two established apple trees near a flower strip or herb spiral before expecting fruit.
messages.catalog.kitchen.name: Garden kitchen
messages.catalog.kitchen.description: An outdoor kitchen with a stove, worktop and shelves for preserving the harvest.
messages.catalog.kitchen.why: Preserving turns summer abundance into winter gifts — jam, sauerkraut and dried herbs keep the sharing table full all year.
messages.catalog.potato.name: Potatoes
messages.catalog.potato.description: Seed potatoes from the community seed bank — plant in spring, hill up with mulch.
messages.catalog.potato.why: A healthy seed tuber can form several new tubers, but yield varies with variety, weather, water, soil and disease. In warm, wet spells, watch for late blight rather than treating an autumn harvest as guaranteed.
messages.catalog.root.name: Root vegetables
messages.catalog.root.description: Carrots and beets from saved seed — they store all winter in sand.
messages.catalog.root.why: Root crops are winter food security — harvested in autumn, shared long after the beds sleep.
messages.catalog.leafy.name: Leafy greens
messages.catalog.leafy.description: Lettuce, chard and spinach — quick growers for spring and summer salads.
messages.catalog.leafy.why: Greens give the fastest harvest in the garden — sow, cut, share, and they grow back.
messages.catalog.cabbage.name: Cabbage
messages.catalog.cabbage.description: Firm autumn cabbage — the classic crop for the garden kitchen.
messages.catalog.cabbage.why: In the kitchen a cabbage becomes sauerkraut — a jar of summer sunshine that lasts all winter.
messages.catalog.herb.name: Kitchen herbs
messages.catalog.herb.description: Thyme, sage and lavender — cuttings and seed from the community bank.
messages.catalog.herb.why: Herbs feed pollinators in flower and people in the kitchen — fresh in summer, dried for winter.
messages.plantWindow.potato.why: seed potatoes go into warming spring soil and need the whole season to bulk up for an autumn lift.
messages.plantWindow.root.why: carrots and beets are sown while the soil is warm, so the roots can size up before the cold.
messages.plantWindow.leafy.why: salads want mild weather — they bolt in a heat wave and sulk in frost.
messages.plantWindow.cabbage.why: cabbage seedlings go out in spring so the heads can firm up by autumn.
messages.plantWindow.herb.why: herb cuttings only take root in warm, living soil.
messages.plantWindow.appleTree.why: trees are planted while dormant — autumn or early spring, never into summer heat or frozen ground.
messages.plantWindow.hugel.why: you can’t dig a hügel bed into frozen winter ground.
messages.plantWindow.herbSpiral.why: stone-laying and planting need unfrozen, workable ground.
messages.plantWindow.pollinator.why: a flower strip is sown into warm soil so it blooms the same year.
messages.plantWindow.birdHouse.why: nest boxes can go up whenever it is safe, although autumn is ideal; never disturb an active nest.

messages.kitchen.subtitle: What the season gave, kept for when it cannot
messages.kitchen.empty: The shelves are bare. The kitchen only keeps what the garden has already given — harvest something first.
messages.kitchen.holding.prompt: Now decide how it should be kept.
messages.kitchen.community.description: Anything put by can go to the table — even in deep winter, when the beds have nothing left to give.
messages.kitchen.dragHint: Let it go over the tool that should keep it
messages.kitchen.chooseFirst: Take something from the shelf first
messages.kitchen.chooseFirst.detail: Choose what you have grown, then decide how it ought to be kept. Nothing here is wasted by guessing.
messages.kitchen.fresh.leafy: Leafy greens are asking to be eaten, not stored. Every method here would cost more than it saved.
messages.kitchen.station.simmer.name: The cauldron
messages.kitchen.station.simmer.what: A slow fire, a heavy pot, and enough sugar or acid that what you seal will keep.
messages.kitchen.station.simmer.wrong: Heat would break this down long before it preserved it.
messages.kitchen.station.dry.name: The oven
messages.kitchen.station.dry.what: Gentle warmth and moving air, until too little water is left for spoilage to begin.
messages.kitchen.station.dry.wrong: There is too much water held in this to dry it safely — it would spoil before it hardened.
messages.kitchen.station.ferment.name: The crock
messages.kitchen.station.ferment.what: Salt, a weight and patience, while the vegetable makes the acid that keeps it.
messages.kitchen.station.ferment.wrong: Fermenting needs something that will make its own acid under salt. This will not.
messages.kitchen.station.store.name: The cold store
messages.kitchen.station.store.what: Dark, cool and barely damp — some things keep best when they are not processed at all.
messages.kitchen.station.store.wrong: The cold store only holds what is already dense and dormant. This would be lost within the week.
messages.seedBank.title: The seed bank
messages.seedBank.subtitle: Every harvest keeps a little of itself back
messages.seedBank.savedSeed.description: Seed you saved yourself can be sown again without waiting for the season's one packet — and it can be given away, which is the only way seed truly survives.
messages.seedBank.empty: The drawers are empty. Harvest a crop while the seed bank stands in the garden, and a little seed will find its way here.
messages.seedBank.community.description: Seed given away is the only seed that survives a bad year. Someone else keeps a copy for you.
messages.seedBank.note.locked.title: The table is not open yet
messages.seedBank.note.locked.text: Sharing opens in the community act, once the garden has soil, water, food and habitat of its own.
messages.seedBank.note.shared.title: A packet went to the table
messages.seedLore.potato.keeps: Saved as whole seed tubers, kept frost-free and dark until the soil warms.
messages.seedLore.potato.note: Potatoes are grown from tubers rather than true seed. Certified seed potato reduces the risk of carrying disease into a new bed, which is why gardeners often buy fresh stock rather than saving their own. Late blight spreads quickly in warm, wet weather; do not put infected foliage in a home compost heap, and follow current local disposal guidance.
messages.seedLore.root.keeps: Carrots and beets set seed in their second year, not their first.
messages.seedLore.root.note: A root left in the ground over winter will flower the following summer and set seed then. Both cross readily with relatives nearby, so saved seed does not always come true to the parent.
messages.seedLore.leafy.keeps: Lettuce runs to seed in heat, and the seed is easy to catch.
messages.seedLore.leafy.note: Let one good plant bolt, let the heads dry, and the seed can be rubbed out by hand. Lettuce mostly self-pollinates, which is part of why it is a forgiving place to start saving seed.
messages.seedLore.cabbage.keeps: Brassicas flower in their second year and cross with almost every relative.
messages.seedLore.cabbage.note: Kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and kohlrabi are one species and cross freely with each other — turnip is a different one and does not. Isolation follows the species, not the name on the packet, and the distance you need varies with wind, insects and what your neighbours grow — a reason seed libraries and hand pollination exist at all.
messages.seedLore.herb.keeps: Most culinary herbs give seed generously at the end of summer.
messages.seedLore.herb.note: Dill, coriander and chervil set seed within one season and are among the simplest to save. Perennial herbs are more often divided or struck from cuttings than grown from seed.

messages.wildlife.heading: Who might visit your garden
messages.wildlife.description: Food, water, shelter and living soil can make visits more likely; wildlife is never guaranteed. Hover a tile to explore useful habitat clues.
messages.wildlife.worm.name: Earthworms
messages.wildlife.worm.tip: Organic matter and moist, undisturbed cover can support earthworms
messages.wildlife.worm.why: Organic matter and surface cover may support earthworms, although populations also depend on soil type, moisture, temperature and species. Their burrows and casts can contribute to soil structure and nutrient cycling.
messages.wildlife.wineCap.name: Wine cap
messages.wildlife.wineCap.tip: Cultivated wine caps need verified spawn, suitable wood chips and moisture
messages.wildlife.wineCap.why: Wine-cap mycelium introduced as verified spawn may colonise suitable untreated wood chips; fruiting is never guaranteed. Never identify or eat a mushroom from this game or from appearance alone.
messages.wildlife.oyster.name: Oyster
messages.wildlife.oyster.tip: Cultivated oysters need verified spawn on suitable untreated wood
messages.wildlife.oyster.why: Verified oyster spawn may digest suitable dead wood under the right moisture and temperature. Buried logs do not automatically produce edible mushrooms. Never use this game to identify food.
messages.wildlife.fieldCap.name: Field cap
messages.wildlife.fieldCap.tip: Wild fungi may appear where soil, weather and organic matter suit them
messages.wildlife.fieldCap.why: A fruiting body may reveal fungal activity underground, but it is not a simple score of soil health. Wild mushrooms can be poisonous: never identify or eat one from this game or appearance alone.
messages.wildlife.bee.name: Bees
messages.wildlife.bee.tip: Flowers plus a clean, shallow drinking place can support visiting bees
messages.wildlife.bee.why: A long flowering season and safe shallow water may support visiting bees. A closed rain barrel is not a drinking source, and pollination varies with crop, weather and the insects present.
messages.wildlife.butterfly.name: Butterflies
messages.wildlife.butterfly.tip: Adults need nectar; caterpillars need the right host plant for their species
messages.wildlife.butterfly.why: Nectar flowers may feed adults, but each butterfly species also needs particular larval host plants — such as nettles for peacocks and many tortoiseshells. A generic “wild corner” cannot meet every species’ needs.
messages.wildlife.bird.name: Birds
messages.wildlife.bird.tip: Clean shallow water and a safe nest box may suit some bird species
messages.wildlife.bird.why: Some cavity-nesting birds may use a correctly designed box and clean shallow water. A closed rain barrel is not a drinking place, and every species has different food, territory and nesting needs.
messages.wildlife.hedgehog.name: Hedgehog
messages.wildlife.hedgehog.tip: Connected access, undisturbed cover and varied invertebrate food may help hedgehogs
messages.wildlife.hedgehog.why: Connected, pesticide-free cover can make a garden safer for night-time foraging and rest. Hedgehogs eat a varied diet that may include beetles, caterpillars and some slugs; no single feature guarantees a visit.
messages.wildlife.ladybug.name: Ladybugs
messages.wildlife.ladybug.tip: Prey, flowering food and suitable dry crevices may support some ladybug species
messages.wildlife.ladybug.why: Some ladybug species may use prey-rich plants, pollen or nectar and dry shelter. Many larvae and adults eat aphids, but species, appetite and overwintering habits vary.
messages.wildlife.beetle.name: Beetles
messages.wildlife.beetle.tip: Undisturbed ground cover can support a diverse range of beetles
messages.wildlife.beetle.why: Many ground beetles shelter under logs, stones or leaf litter and forage at night. Diets differ widely: some eat invertebrates, some seeds and some both, so their effects cannot be reduced to “pest control”.
messages.visit.defer: Not now — let them visit later
messages.visit.lost.close: Adjust the habitat and try later
messages.visit.hedgehog.intro: a hedgehog shuffled out of the neighbour’s hedge and is sniffing at your gate!
messages.visit.hedgehog.question: You want to leave it a welcome saucer. What must NEVER be in it?
messages.visit.hedgehog.fact: Milk and bread can make hedgehogs ill. Fresh water is the safest everyday help; meaty cat or dog food may be used only as supplementary food, never as a replacement for a healthy habitat.
messages.visit.bird.intro: a robin keeps landing on the neighbour’s fence, watching your beds with interest!
messages.visit.bird.question: Pick the 3 foods a robin can safely find or be offered in your garden:
messages.visit.bird.fact: Robins hunt invertebrates and berries. Salt is toxic to birds, they cannot digest milk — and whole peanuts can choke chicks in spring.
messages.visit.bee.intro: a honeybee scout is circling the neighbour’s lavender — and just noticed your garden!
messages.visit.bee.question: Back at the hive she performs the waggle dance. What does it tell the other bees?
messages.visit.bee.option.0: Direction AND distance to the flowers
messages.visit.bee.fact: The dance angle mirrors the sun’s direction and the waggle length encodes distance — a map, danced in the dark of the hive.
messages.visit.butterfly.intro: a peacock butterfly is sunning itself on the neighbour’s wall, eyeing your flowers!
messages.visit.butterfly.question: Peacock and tortoiseshell butterflies lay their eggs almost ONLY on…
messages.visit.butterfly.fact: Stinging nettle is the main larval food plant for peacocks and many tortoiseshells. Other butterfly species need different host plants, so nectar flowers alone are not enough.
messages.visit.ladybug.intro: a ladybug landed on the neighbour’s bean poles — one hop from your garden!
messages.visit.ladybug.question: Before it pupates, one ladybug LARVA eats about how many of these aphids?
messages.visit.ladybug.fact: A ladybug larva can consume hundreds of aphids while developing, although appetite varies by species and conditions. Diverse habitat supports predators more safely than broad pesticide.
messages.visit.worm.intro: the neighbour’s compost is full of earthworms — and your covered soil may suit some of them!
messages.visit.worm.question: Darwin estimated that worms brought roughly how much fine earth to the surface each year in some English pasture?
messages.visit.worm.fact: Darwin’s figure converts to roughly 20–25 tonnes per hectare each year in the pastures he studied. Rates vary greatly with soil, climate, land use and worm abundance.
messages.visit.wineCap.intro: a neighbour offers verified wine-cap spawn for a fresh wood-chip bed. Safety: never identify or eat a wild mushroom from this game or appearance alone.
messages.visit.wineCap.question: Wine cap mushrooms fruit best on…
messages.visit.wineCap.fact: Verified wine-cap spawn can colonise suitable untreated wood chips when moisture and temperature cooperate. Fruiting time varies and is not guaranteed. Never eat a mushroom identified only by an app or picture.
messages.visit.oyster.intro: a neighbour offers verified oyster spawn for suitable untreated wood. Safety: never identify or eat a wild mushroom from this game or appearance alone.
messages.visit.oyster.question: Oyster mushrooms are secret hunters — their mycelium traps and eats…
messages.visit.oyster.fact: Oyster mycelium can immobilise tiny nematodes and obtain nutrients from them while also decomposing wood. Cultivation still requires verified spawn and correct conditions; this fact is not an identification guide.
messages.visit.fieldCap.intro: a ring of unidentified wild mushrooms appeared on the neighbour’s lawn. Safety: observe them, but never identify or eat one from this game or appearance alone.
messages.visit.fieldCap.question: That “fairy ring” of mushrooms reveals…
messages.visit.fieldCap.option.0: The fungus growing outward underground, year by year
messages.visit.fieldCap.fact: A ring can form as fungal mycelium expands through the soil, although rings have several possible causes and ages. It does not identify the species or prove that the mushrooms are edible.
messages.visit.beetle.intro: a ground beetle scuttled under the neighbour’s gate at dusk — hunting season!
messages.visit.beetle.question: Where does a ground beetle hide through the day before its night hunts?
messages.visit.beetle.fact: Many ground beetles shelter beneath mulch, stones or logs and forage at night. Diets vary by species: some eat insect larvae or slug eggs, while others also eat seeds.
messages.community.heading: Community sharing table
messages.community.kicker: Take what you need, let the rest circulate — an economy of gifts.
messages.community.giveZone.hint: Drag a garden element here — or click me, then click an element on the plot
messages.community.quiet: Quiet right now — tap “See who's sharing today”.
messages.community.locked.title: The sharing table is still ahead
messages.community.locked.text: Care for soil, water, food and habitat first. The community table opens when your garden can offer a genuine surplus.
messages.community.disclaimer: “Shares” are game tokens for participation. A real fair share may be time, care, knowledge, access or surplus, without expecting equal repayment.
messages.community.pool.explanation: A transparent learning-game estimate: giving grows the shared pool; taking uses it.
messages.community.freshRule: Fresh produce is shared in its season — preserves keep for winter gifts.

messages.winter.bee: overwintering in species-specific ways — a colony, adult, larva or pupa
messages.winter.butterfly: overwintering in a species-specific stage — egg, caterpillar, chrysalis or adult
messages.winter.hedgehog: possibly hibernating in a quiet, well-built shelter
messages.winter.ladybug: sheltering in dry crevices, leaf litter or other protected places
messages.winter.beetle: sheltering in soil, litter or dead wood, depending on species
messages.winter.wineCap: remaining as mycelium while fruiting pauses

messages.season.spring.name: Spring
messages.season.spring.tip: 🌸 Spring changes the garden — more wildlife activity may become visible, while the sharing table fills with seedlings and prunings. Wake established no-dig beds gently with a surface layer of mature compost.
messages.season.spring.passage.title: The soil loosens its breath
messages.season.spring.passage.voice: The frost has loosened its hold. New companions arrive carefully, and last year’s rain rises through the soil.
messages.season.summer.name: Summer
messages.season.summer.tip: ☀️ Summer brings vigorous growth and many visible relationships. The table offers grass clippings and green material; suitable mulch helps slow soil-water loss, while safely stored rain can bridge dry weeks.
messages.season.summer.passage.title: Everything asks for relationship
messages.season.summer.passage.voice: My leaves are full of light. Water, shade and many kinds of flower decide whether abundance can keep its balance.
messages.season.autumn.name: Autumn
messages.season.autumn.tip: 🍂 Autumn is the gift season — rake fallen leaves for compost, harvest mature fruit and decide what to eat, preserve or share. Gifts strengthen the pool rather than repaying the giver.
messages.season.autumn.passage.title: A gift becomes tomorrow
messages.season.autumn.passage.voice: Fruit, leaves and seed are arriving together. What is shared, stored or returned now will shape the quiet months.
messages.season.winter.name: Winter
messages.season.winter.tip: ❄️ Winter changes, rather than empties, the garden. Different species overwinter in different stages and places; resident birds and subtle signs of soil life may remain. The table offers wood, prunings and stored materials, while mulch protects the soil surface.
messages.season.winter.passage.title: Quiet is another kind of work
messages.season.winter.passage.voice: I have drawn my energy inward. Beneath cover and bark, many lives wait without becoming absent.
messages.guild.heading: Design connections
messages.guild.review: A design connection in your garden
messages.guild.voice: You looked between the elements. That is where my strongest design lives.
messages.guild.hotbed.name: Hot-bed idea
messages.guild.hotbed.what: Compost beside a greenhouse suggests a hot-bed experiment — but an ordinary bin outside will not heat the seedlings.
messages.guild.hotbed.why: A real hot bed uses a large, actively decomposing mass beneath or inside an insulated frame. It needs suitable material, ventilation and temperature monitoring before plants are added.
messages.guild.hotbed.who: Heat-loving seedlings may benefit once a real hot bed is safely built and its temperature has stabilised.
messages.guild.dripCorner.name: Drip corner
messages.guild.dripCorner.what: A nearby rain barrel could feed the herb spiral through a carefully connected gravity line.
messages.guild.dripCorner.why: Gravity irrigation works only when the covered barrel is stable, raised safely and connected to a controlled outlet. Keep overflow safe and match each herb to the spiral’s actual moisture.
messages.guild.dripCorner.who: Flowering herbs may support visiting bees and hoverflies when water is delivered safely.
messages.guild.foodForest.name: Food forest corner
messages.guild.foodForest.what: A layered woody bed beneath a climbing arch could grow food at two heights in one footprint.
messages.guild.foodForest.why: Vertical layers can add edges and microclimates, but yields depend on light, water, soil and crop choice. Observe whether the pairing works in this place.
messages.guild.foodForest.who: Soil organisms below and visiting birds above may use different parts of the layered habitat.
messages.guild.pollinatorPair.name: Pollinator paradise
messages.guild.pollinatorPair.what: Suitable nesting cavities beside a long-flowering strip may offer food and shelter to some solitary insects.
messages.guild.pollinatorPair.why: A dry, well-built hotel can help some species when the right flowers and nesting materials are present. It neither guarantees residents nor automatically increases every crop yield.
messages.guild.pollinatorPair.who: Some solitary bees and other insects may find suitable food or nesting space.
messages.guild.seedLibrary.name: Living seed library
messages.guild.seedLibrary.what: A seed bank beside flowering plants invites careful observation of pollination, maturity and seed harvest.
messages.guild.seedLibrary.why: Open-pollinated seed selected over generations may develop useful local traits, but isolation, population size and accidental crossing must be managed.
messages.guild.seedLibrary.who: Pollinating insects may visit the flowering strip; seed savers still need to manage crossing.
messages.guild.classroom.name: Outdoor classroom
messages.guild.classroom.what: A bench beside the garden sign — a place to sit, read and learn.
messages.guild.classroom.why: Care for people: a garden that teaches builds the community that sustains it.
messages.guild.classroom.who: People — the community that keeps the garden alive.
messages.guild.nectarCover.name: Nectar and cover
messages.guild.nectarCover.what: Flowers beside undisturbed mulch may feed and shelter the same insects at different stages of their lives.
messages.guild.nectarCover.why: Many beneficial insects need more than nectar — somewhere to overwinter, to pupate, or to shelter between meals. Flowering plants next to ground that is not dug can cover more of that cycle than either does alone, although which species benefit depends on the plants, the mulch and what surrounds the garden.
messages.guild.nectarCover.who: Hoverflies, solitary bees and ground beetles may use the two together, at different points in their year.
messages.guild.birdNeighbours.name: Bird neighbours
messages.guild.birdNeighbours.what: A suitable nest box near a growing bed may give some cavity-nesting birds access to varied foraging habitat.
messages.guild.birdNeighbours.why: Many garden birds feed chicks a range of invertebrates, but they are wild neighbours rather than guaranteed pest control. Diverse habitat and direct crop protection still matter.
messages.guild.birdNeighbours.who: Some birds may nest or forage nearby; their diets and effects vary by species and season.
messages.resident.hedgehog.name: The hedgehog
messages.resident.hedgehog.1.title: Something crossed in the night
messages.resident.hedgehog.1.text: Something moved through the leaf litter last night. Small, unhurried, certain of its way. I did not plant it and I cannot keep it — but the cover you left made the crossing possible.
messages.resident.hedgehog.2.title: It stayed through the cold
messages.resident.hedgehog.2.text: Under the wood and the mulch, through the coldest weeks, something slept and did not die. That is not luck alone. You left the corner undisturbed when tidying it would have been easier.
messages.resident.hedgehog.3.title: Smaller tracks beside the old ones
messages.resident.hedgehog.3.text: There are smaller prints now beside the first. I will not promise you they all live out the year — I cannot, and neither can anyone. But a garden safe enough to sleep in has become a garden safe enough to raise young in. That is the whole of it.
messages.resident.bee.name: The bees
messages.resident.bee.1.title: The flowers were found
messages.resident.bee.1.text: Something came from somewhere else and decided this was worth the journey. I did not call it. Word travels here in a language of scent and distance.
messages.resident.bee.2.title: Something has stayed open
messages.resident.bee.2.text: For weeks now, as one flower closed another was already waiting. That continuity is far harder to design than a single beautiful bed — and you built it without being asked to.
messages.resident.bee.3.title: The circle closes
messages.resident.bee.3.text: Fruit is setting where the flowers stood. I cannot tell you which visit made which fruit — that is not how any of this works. But the visitors came, the harvest followed, and both belong to the same arrangement.
messages.resident.worm.name: The earthworms
messages.resident.worm.1.title: Work you will never watch
messages.resident.worm.1.text: Beneath the cover something began that you will almost never see. Organic matter and a little shade were invitation enough.
messages.resident.worm.2.title: The ground opens
messages.resident.worm.2.text: Rain sinks differently now. Burrows and castings change where water goes and how far roots may follow. Slowly — soil keeps its own time, not ours.
messages.resident.worm.3.title: Alive under the frost
messages.resident.worm.3.text: Even through the cold months, under the mulch, the work did not stop entirely. You have made something that no longer needs you to be watching it.
messages.pest.heading: The garden is out of balance
messages.pest.aphid.name: Aphids
messages.pest.aphid.reading: nothing here hunts them, and nothing that would could stay the winter
messages.pest.aphid.relief: Rinse the shoot tips with water
messages.pest.aphid.reliefWhy: Plain water dislodges many of them and touches nothing else that lives here. The stems will be found again while the cause remains.
messages.pest.aphid.1.title: Something is feeding on the new growth
messages.pest.aphid.1.text: The softest shoots are curling. Something small has found them, and there are many — they arrive faster than anything here can answer. I am not telling you this to alarm you. I am telling you because you asked to see what I see.
messages.pest.aphid.2.title: What is missing is not a remedy
messages.pest.aphid.2.text: You could ask what will remove them. I would rather tell you what is absent. Nothing here hunts them. There is no long flowering season to hold a predator between meals, and no dry crevice for one to pass the winter in. The aphids are not the problem — they are the reading.
messages.pest.aphid.3.title: Something came to meet them
messages.pest.aphid.3.text: There are ladybugs on the same stems now. I cannot tell you they will clear every one, and I would not want them to — a predator that finishes its prey has nowhere left to live. What you built was not a weapon. It was a place for something to stay long enough to matter.
messages.pest.slug.name: Slugs
messages.pest.slug.reading: the cover holds water and hides them, and nothing forages here after dark
messages.pest.slug.relief: Lift the boards at dusk and move them on
messages.pest.slug.reliefWhy: Collecting by hand at dusk works and harms nothing else. It also has to be done again every week the cause remains.
messages.pest.slug.1.title: Silver trails across the leaves
messages.pest.slug.1.text: By morning the young leaves had holes, and the trails were still bright across the soil. The damp cover you laid is good for much of what lives here. It is good for this, too.
messages.pest.slug.2.title: Shelter without a hunter
messages.pest.slug.2.text: Mulch holds water, feeds the soil and hides the slugs from the sun. All of that is one decision, not three. What this garden does not yet have is anything that forages here at night — no undisturbed corner, no ground cover deep enough, no reason for a night visitor to make the crossing. Shelter without a hunter is only shelter for one side.
messages.pest.slug.3.title: The nights are busier now
messages.pest.slug.3.text: Something works through the litter after dark. Slugs are still here — they will be, and that is not failure. Hedgehogs, birds and ground beetles eat many things, and the balance they keep is never a clean sweep. Fewer holes in the leaves is all I can honestly report. It is enough.
messages.pest.caterpillar.name: Caterpillars
messages.pest.caterpillar.reading: nothing includes these rows in its morning
messages.pest.caterpillar.relief: Check the undersides and lift them off
messages.pest.caterpillar.reliefWhy: Going leaf by leaf works on a small plot and takes only patience. It changes nothing about why they were the only ones looking.
messages.pest.caterpillar.1.title: Eaten from the inside out
messages.pest.caterpillar.1.text: White butterflies came to the brassicas, and what they left behind is feeding now. It is easy to resent this. I would rather you look at it first — the same wings you welcomed among the flowers laid these eggs. They were never two different visitors.
messages.pest.caterpillar.2.title: No one is working these rows
messages.pest.caterpillar.2.text: Caterpillars are food. That is not a comfort — it is a fact this garden cannot yet use, because nothing here is hunting them. No nest box, no clean shallow water, no reason for a bird to include these rows in its morning.
messages.pest.caterpillar.3.title: The rows are on someone’s route
messages.pest.caterpillar.3.text: Birds work the brassicas in the early hours now. Some caterpillars will still finish, become butterflies and return to the flowers, which is how it should go. You did not remove anything from this garden. You added the part that was missing, and the rest arranged itself.
messages.book.title: The garden book
messages.book.subtitle: Everything the garden can teach you
messages.book.intro: what each part does, why it matters and what it may support. Nothing here is a promise — gardens differ.
messages.book.tab.elements.label: Elements
messages.book.tab.elements.intro: Everything you can place in the garden — what it is, why it matters, and which lives it may support.
messages.book.tab.wildlife.label: Who may visit
messages.book.tab.wildlife.intro: Neighbours who may arrive when conditions suit them. None of them are promised; gardens differ.
messages.book.tab.guilds.label: Connections
messages.book.tab.guilds.intro: Pairwise design connections between elements. A full plant guild usually weaves several compatible species and functions together; one nearby pair is only a beginning.
messages.book.tab.principles.label: Principles
messages.book.tab.principles.intro: The lessons the garden teaches through its challenges — observation before action.
messages.book.tab.balance.label: Balance
messages.book.tab.balance.intro: When something multiplies beyond what the rest can absorb, it is describing an absence. These pages are about reading that, not about winning against it.
messages.book.tab.keeping.label: Keeping
messages.book.tab.keeping.intro: A season gives more than a week can eat. These pages are about the two ways a garden carries itself forward — food kept, and seed kept.
messages.book.keeping.why.name: Why anything is kept at all
messages.book.keeping.why.description: Abundance arrives all at once. Hunger does not.
messages.book.keeping.why.text: Every method of keeping food does one thing: it makes the harvest available at a time the garden cannot supply it. Sugar, acid, salt, drying and cold all work by making conditions difficult for the organisms that would otherwise consume the food first. Which method suits which crop is not a matter of taste — it follows from what the crop is made of. This game models the choice, not the practice: for anything you intend to eat, follow a current tested guide rather than a garden story.
messages.book.keeping.simmer.name: Simmering and sealing
messages.book.keeping.simmer.description: Heat, sugar or acid, and a seal that holds.
messages.book.keeping.simmer.text: Fruit preserves rely on heat plus enough sugar or acidity to keep spoilage organisms from growing. Low-acid foods are a different matter entirely and need equipment and methods this game does not model. Follow a tested, current preserving guide for anything you intend to eat — never a game.
messages.book.keeping.dry.name: Drying
messages.book.keeping.dry.description: Take the water away and most spoilage simply cannot begin.
messages.book.keeping.dry.text: Gentle warmth and moving air remove the moisture that microbes need. It suits thin slices and leafy herbs, and suits watery vegetables poorly. Dried food still needs dry, dark, airtight storage — drying delays spoilage, it does not end it.
messages.book.keeping.ferment.name: Fermenting
messages.book.keeping.ferment.description: The vegetable makes the acid that keeps it.
messages.book.keeping.ferment.text: Under salt and without air, lactic acid bacteria already present on the vegetable produce acid that preserves it. It suits cabbage and many roots. Salt ratio, temperature and keeping everything below the brine all matter; consult a current, tested guide before eating anything you have fermented.
messages.book.keeping.store.name: Simply keeping
messages.book.keeping.store.description: Some crops need no processing at all — only the right dark.
messages.book.keeping.store.text: Potatoes and many roots can keep for months when stored correctly, but they do not want identical conditions. Keep potatoes cool, dark, dry and ventilated; light, damage and sprouting can raise natural glycoalkaloids, so do not eat green, sprouted or bitter parts. Many roots prefer a slightly damper store such as sand. Check every crop regularly and follow current food-safety guidance.
messages.book.keeping.seed.name: Keeping seed
messages.book.keeping.seed.description: The only harvest that makes next year possible.
messages.book.keeping.seed.text: Seed saved from your own garden is adapted a little to your own ground, and costs nothing to sow again. How easily it comes true varies enormously: lettuce mostly selfs and is forgiving, brassicas cross with every relative nearby, and biennials like carrot only flower in their second year. Seed given away is also the only seed that survives a bad year in one garden.
messages.book.balance.reading.name: The problem is the solution
messages.book.balance.reading.description: An outbreak names what a garden is missing. Removing the outbreak does not supply it.
messages.book.balance.reading.text: A species that multiplies beyond what the rest of the system can absorb is usually revealing an absence — of predators, of diversity, or of the habitat that lets a predator stay between meals. Treat only the symptom and the garden returns to the same arrangement that produced it. This is a way of reading a garden, not a guarantee: some problems are weather, some are soil, and some simply take longer than one season to answer.
messages.book.balance.aphid.name: Aphids and their predators
messages.book.balance.aphid.description: A sudden rise in aphid numbers is information about the garden, not only about the aphids.
messages.book.balance.aphid.text: Aphid populations can build very quickly in warm weather. Where a long flowering season and dry overwintering cavities exist, predators such as some ladybird species, hoverfly larvae and lacewings may be present as well — although which species arrive, and how much difference they make, varies with place, weather and season. Broad pesticide treatments reduce those predators too, which is why an outbreak often returns worse after them.
messages.book.balance.slug.name: Slugs and night foragers
messages.book.balance.slug.description: Damp cover is good for soil life. It is also good for slugs — one decision does both.
messages.book.balance.slug.text: Mulch slows evaporation and feeds soil organisms while also giving slugs daytime shelter. Hedgehogs, some birds and many ground beetles may include slugs in varied diets, though how much any of them eat varies by species, season and what else is available — none specialise in slugs and none will remove them. Collecting by hand at dusk is effective on a small plot and harms nothing else; it treats the symptom rather than the arrangement that allows it.
messages.book.balance.caterpillar.name: Caterpillars and the same wings
messages.book.balance.caterpillar.description: The butterflies welcomed among the flowers are the ones that lay on the brassicas.
messages.book.balance.caterpillar.text: Large and small white butterflies feed on nectar as adults and lay eggs on brassicas, where the caterpillars feed. Insect-eating birds may take caterpillars, particularly while raising young, though this depends on species, season and what else is available. Netting of a suitable mesh keeps the butterflies off without harming them. None of this makes the butterfly an enemy — it is the same visitor at a different stage.
messages.systems.heading: Relationships, not checkboxes
messages.systems.modelNote: A learning-game model of useful connections, not a scientific measurement of a real garden.
messages.systems.soil.name: Living soil
messages.systems.soil.reason.present: Organic matter is feeding the soil.
messages.systems.soil.reason.missing: Bare soil has little protection yet.
messages.systems.water.name: Water security
messages.systems.water.link: Stored rain feeds a nearby growing area
messages.systems.water.reason.connected: Stored rain is close enough to serve plants.
messages.systems.water.reason.stored: Rain is stored; connect it to a growing area.
messages.systems.water.reason.drinkingOnly: Wildlife has drinking water, but rain is not being stored yet.
messages.systems.water.reason.missing: No rainwater is being caught yet.
messages.systems.food.name: Food web
messages.systems.food.reason.connected: Flowers and food crops reinforce each other.
messages.systems.food.reason.present: Food is growing; add flowering partners.
messages.systems.food.reason.missing: No edible layer is growing yet.
messages.systems.habitat.name: Habitat
messages.systems.habitat.link: Shelter connects with a feeding area
messages.systems.habitat.reason.connected: Food and shelter form a connected refuge.
messages.systems.habitat.reason.present: Some shelter exists; connect it to food and water.
messages.reflection.heading: The garden reflects
messages.reflection.three.voice: I can feel soil, water and food beginning to answer one another. Resilience grows in the conversation between them.
messages.reflection.three.note: Three living layers are now present. The next step is to make room for other species, then let a real surplus circulate.
messages.reflection.share.voice: You made room for lives you may never meet, then let one gift continue beyond my gate.
messages.reflection.share.note: Care for earth, care for people and fair share are becoming one system rather than three separate tasks.
messages.gardenVoice.guild: You looked between the elements. That is where my strongest design lives.
messages.gardenVoice.ending: You did not finish me. You helped me become able to continue — through another season, another visitor and another gift.
messages.livingLesson.card.title: Ask what the garden notices
messages.livingLesson.card.description: A short reflection becomes one testable design experiment. The garden rules stay deterministic.
messages.livingLesson.dialog.title: The garden reflects
messages.livingLesson.dialog.subtitle: The garden has looked at what you have made and found one thing worth trying.
messages.livingLesson.dialog.attribution: Its words come from GPT-5.6 Luna; the garden’s rules stay its own.
messages.livingLesson.loading.detail: The garden is reading relationships, not judging your score.
messages.livingLesson.section.question: A question to carry
messages.livingLesson.section.action: One small action beyond the screen
messages.livingLesson.trust.detail: Only a small anonymous snapshot of this garden was used. GPT‑5.6 Luna can shape this reflection, but it cannot change game rules, scores, prices or success conditions. When AI is unavailable, the same feature continues with reviewed garden wisdom.
messages.livingLesson.locked.label: ✦ Ask after two learning acts
messages.livingLesson.locked.hint: Finish any two learning acts first, so the garden has something of yours to look at.
messages.livingLesson.active.label: ✦ The garden is still watching
messages.livingLesson.active.hint: Finish what the garden already asked of you, then ask again.
messages.livingLesson.ready.label: ✦ Ask the garden for help
messages.livingLesson.ready.hint: The garden looks at your plot and offers one thing worth trying.
messages.livingLesson.again.label: ✦ Ask the garden again
messages.livingLesson.error.locked: Let soil and water begin their conversation first — complete two learning acts, then listen again.
messages.livingLesson.error.active: The garden is still waiting on what it already asked of you. Change something, then come back.
messages.livingLesson.toast.started: ✦ The garden asked something of you
messages.livingLesson.toast.completed: ✦ The garden saw it. What you changed is now part of what it knows.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.soil.observation: My quietest work is happening underfoot.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.soil.relationship: Soil life grows through cover, organic matter and time; nearby mulch helps roots keep moisture while decomposition feeds the web.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.water.observation: I notice where each drop can pause, and where it still has nowhere useful to go.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.water.relationship: Catching rain is only the first step; stored water becomes part of a system when it is safely directed toward soil and plants.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.food.observation: A harvest is strongest when it is held by more than one relationship.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.food.relationship: Edible layers, flowering plants and seed stewardship can reinforce one another across the season.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.habitat.observatio: Some neighbours arrive only when food, water and shelter meet.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.habitat.relationsh: Habitat works as a connected refuge; one isolated shelter cannot guarantee wildlife, but it can improve the conditions they need.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.sharing.observatio: What leaves my gate can become another beginning.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.sharing.relationsh: Fair share is the circulation of genuine surplus, care or knowledge, without requiring an equal return.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.relationships.obse: Look between the elements, not only at the elements themselves.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.relationships.rela: Placement turns separate objects into useful relationships: a need in one place can be met by a yield from another.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.season.observation: A season does not judge the design; it reveals what the design can learn.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.season.relationshi: Observation after change helps a gardener adapt instead of assuming that one arrangement will always work.
messages.livingLesson.fallback.question.sharing: What genuine surplus can move onward without weakening the garden?

messages.challenge.mulch.title: Soil moisture rescue
messages.challenge.mulch.story: A hot afternoon is coming. You have four barrows of mulch and six bare beds, so observation matters before action.
messages.challenge.mulch.prompt: Read the moisture tags and protect the four thirsty beds first. Beds above 50% can wait until the next barrow arrives.
messages.challenge.mulch.skill: reading soil moisture and prioritising water
messages.challenge.mulch.lesson: Mulch shades soil, slows evaporation and feeds soil life. Most cultivated beds benefit from suitable cover; when materials are scarce, observe first and protect the driest, most exposed soil.
messages.challenge.mulch.impact: The mulch practice now supports a mulch element while it remains in the garden.
messages.challenge.compost.title: Feed the compost
messages.challenge.compost.story: You are starting a fresh compost pile. A varied first mix needs moist, nitrogen-rich greens plus dry, carbon-rich browns, with space for air.
messages.challenge.compost.prompt: Choose exactly four ingredients: two greens and two browns. Leave contaminants out, then build this new pile.
messages.challenge.compost.skill: balancing carbon, nitrogen, air and moisture
messages.challenge.compost.lesson: A new pile can begin with a varied mix of greens and browns, then be adjusted by observation. An existing cold, soggy pile usually needs dry browns, aeration and protection from excess rain — not more wet greens. Local compost rules may differ.
messages.challenge.compost.feedback.count: Choose exactly four ingredients before building the pile.
messages.challenge.compost.feedback.balance: The pile needs balance: two moist greens and two dry browns.
messages.challenge.compost.impact: The balanced-compost practice now supports a compost element while it remains in the garden.
messages.challenge.hugel.title: Test a layered wood bed
messages.challenge.hugel.story: Suitable untreated woody material can be tested in a raised bed instead of removed. Results vary with soil, climate, wood, construction and time.
messages.challenge.hugel.prompt: Build one common layer sequence from the ground up, then plan to monitor settling, moisture and plant growth rather than assuming success.
messages.challenge.hugel.lesson: Logs, branches, organic matter, compost and soil are one common sequence — not a proven universal recipe. Avoid treated, diseased or invasive wood, expect settling and observe whether the bed actually helps in your conditions.

messages.challenge.rain.title: Guide every drop
messages.challenge.rain.story: The next shower should fill more than a barrel. A safe system collects water from a suitable roof and gives the overflow somewhere useful to go.
messages.challenge.rain.prompt: Complete the water journey in the right order, from the roof edge to soil that can absorb the overflow.
messages.challenge.rain.lesson: Guide suitable roof water through a gutter and screen into a stable, securely covered barrel, then send overflow to a safe infiltration area. Treat stored roof water as non-potable, follow local rules and use mosquito screening; roof materials affect where the water is safe to use.

messages.challenge.kitchen.title: Plan the winter pantry
messages.challenge.kitchen.story: The harvest table is overflowing, but every crop keeps best in a different way. A thoughtful pantry carries summer abundance into winter.
messages.challenge.kitchen.prompt: Choose the best use or preservation method for each crate. A wrong choice reveals a clue, so you can rethink it.
messages.challenge.kitchen.lesson: Jam fruit, dry apples and herbs, ferment cabbage, cellar roots and share tender leaves while they are fresh. Diversity in the pantry reduces waste.

messages.challenge.kitchen.why.cherries: Cherries make a bright preserve when cooked as jam.
messages.challenge.kitchen.why.apples: Apple slices dry well and keep with very little energy.
messages.challenge.kitchen.why.cabbage: Salt and time turn cabbage into a stable ferment.
messages.challenge.kitchen.why.leafy: Tender leaves lose quality quickly, so share them fresh.
messages.challenge.kitchen.why.roots: Cool, dark storage keeps roots firm for months.
messages.challenge.kitchen.impact: The preservation plan supports food continuity while the kitchen remains in the garden.
messages.challenge.ladybug.title: Restore the balance
messages.challenge.ladybug.story: Aphids have appeared on the young leaves. The goal is not to erase every insect, but to rebuild the relationships that keep outbreaks in check.
messages.challenge.ladybug.prompt: Select the three actions that support ladybugs, hoverflies and other natural predators, then restore balance.
messages.challenge.ladybug.lesson: Flowering plants feed adult predators, hollow stems offer shelter and patient observation gives them time to respond. Broad pesticides break this balance.
messages.challenge.ladybug.feedback.count: Choose three actions before checking the plan.
messages.challenge.ladybug.impact: The predator-support plan works while flowers and insect shelter remain connected.
messages.challenge.bee.title: Keep the nectar flowing
messages.challenge.bee.story: A colourful flower bed can still leave pollinators hungry if everything blooms in the same month. The missing dimension is time.
messages.challenge.bee.prompt: Build a three-season nectar calendar. Match one plant to spring, summer and autumn so food never disappears.
messages.challenge.bee.lesson: Willow catkins feed early pollinators, borage carries them through summer and ivy flowers provide vital late nectar in autumn.
messages.challenge.bee.impact: The nectar-calendar plan works while flowering support remains connected to food.
messages.challenge.shelter.title: Make room for winter
messages.challenge.shelter.story: The first hard frost is tonight. Each small garden worker needs a different kind of quiet, dry or living refuge.
messages.challenge.shelter.prompt: Find the most suitable winter home for each animal. The clues are in how they live and feed.
messages.challenge.shelter.lesson: Undisturbed leaf piles can shelter hedgehogs, hollow stems protect some overwintering insects, active compost buffers soil organisms and dense woody corners can hold butterfly chrysalises.

messages.challenge.shelter.impact: The winter-refuge plan works while habitat remains in the garden.
messages.challenge.connections.title: Complete the connection
messages.challenge.connections.story: One useful pair is the beginning of a design connection. A fuller plant guild weaves several compatible species and functions together.
messages.challenge.connections.prompt: For each familiar garden element, choose the partner that completes a useful connection you have already discovered.
messages.challenge.connections.lesson: A proposed connection links possible needs and yields — heat, water, shelter, food or learning — but each relationship remains a hypothesis to observe and adjust on the real site. A full guild combines several such roles.
messages.challenge.connections.impact: Relationship-design insight recorded — knowledge changes your next decision, not a physical meter.
messages.challenge.seeds.title: Choose tomorrow’s seeds
messages.challenge.seeds.story: The seed library needs well-labelled seed — not simply the biggest handful. Start with suitable open-pollinated plants, then consider maturity, dryness, population size, isolation and health.
messages.challenge.seeds.prompt: Inspect each simplified seed batch and decide whether to store it, wait for better conditions, or reject it. Real crops may require species-specific guidance.
messages.challenge.seeds.skill: reading seed maturity, dryness, health and breeding context
messages.challenge.seeds.lesson: Save fully dry, mature seed from suitable open-pollinated plants. Hybrid offspring may not resemble the parent, and cross-pollinating crops need enough plants and suitable isolation. Disease risk is crop- and pathogen-specific: visibly mouldy seed should not be stored, while a symptom on the parent does not automatically mean every seed is unsafe.

messages.challenge.quiz.title: Read the garden
messages.challenge.quiz.story: The garden rarely presents a neat true-or-false question. It presents a situation, several possible actions and a need to notice the whole system.
messages.challenge.quiz.prompt: Work through three garden situations. Choose the response that solves today’s problem without creating tomorrow’s.
messages.challenge.quiz.skill: systems thinking in everyday garden decisions
messages.challenge.quiz.lesson: Permaculture decisions favour observation, soil cover, living relationships, low disturbance and sharing surplus. The best answer usually solves more than one problem.

messages.community.firstGiftHint: Easiest first gifts: pick ripe produce in season, or let compost, mulch or herbs establish one seasonal turn — they can share a division without leaving your garden.
messages.community.summerGiftHint: In summer, the ripe cherries on your tree are the easiest first gift 🍒 — click a glowing cluster, then share from the basket.
messages.community.shareRealSurplus: Share one genuine surplus, then notice how the shared pool and community care respond.
messages.community.shareFreshProduce: Share the harvested produce, not an unharvested crop.
messages.community.tableFull: The table is already full — take what you need first.
messages.community.checkedTooSoon: You already checked since the last gift or seasonal turn. Let the community rhythm breathe before checking again.
messages.community.poolTooLow: The shared pool is too low for this offering. Let another genuine gift circulate first.
messages.community.newElement: Newly placed — let it establish through one seasonal turn, then it can spare
messages.community.establishedSpare: Established duplicate available as a genuine spare.

messages.kitchen.differentHarvests: Different harvests need different low-energy ways of keeping.
messages.principle.compostSupply: A balanced compost recipe can create a future supply of organic matter.
messages.principle.habitatThroughTime: A habitat must work through time, not only look colourful today.
messages.principle.balanceHabitat: Balance grows from habitat, patience and targeted protection.
messages.principle.everyElement: Every element has needs, yields and neighbours.
messages.principle.winterRefuges: Different lives require different winter refuges.
messages.principle.winterRefugesResult: Different winter refuges now support different kinds of garden life.
messages.principle.seedSelection: Healthy, mature seed from suitable plants has been selected for the next sowing.
messages.principle.soilAction: Cover one small patch of bare soil with leaves, straw or other suitable organic material.
messages.principle.waterAction: Watch one rainfall and notice where water could be slowed or safely collected.
messages.principle.habitatAction: Leave one quiet, pesticide-free refuge with water, food and shelter.
messages.principle.rainSystem: Water should be screened, safely stored and given a planned overflow path.
messages.principle.seedSystem: Save suitable open-pollinated seed with attention to health, maturity and isolation.
messages.principle.woodyBed: Woody beds are site-specific experiments: observe moisture, settling and fertility over time.
messages.principle.woodyBedPoetic: Fallen wood may help the rain linger beneath new roots. Watch what this mound does through dry weather.
messages.principle.woodyBedPast: Wood that had fallen may help rain linger beneath new roots. Watch what the mound does through dry weather.
messages.principle.rainResult: Roof water now has screened storage and a planned overflow route.
messages.principle.rainFlow: The next rain can pause, fill, overflow and sink instead of hurrying away.
messages.principle.rainFlowPoetic: The next rain will pause, fill, overflow and sink — instead of hurrying away.
messages.principle.mulchResult: The driest beds are now covered. Their soil can lose water more slowly in hot weather.
messages.principle.preserveResult: The pantry plan keeps suitable harvests useful beyond their fresh season.
messages.principle.pollinatorResult: The planting plan reduces seasonal gaps in nectar and pollen.
messages.principle.predatorResult: Predators have food and shelter, while young plants receive targeted protection.
messages.principle.futureSeed: Tomorrow’s garden is already folded into a handful of careful seed.
messages.principle.floweringContinuity: One flowering season can now hand its work to the next.
messages.principle.floweringContinuityDone: One flowering season now hands the work to the next.
messages.principle.summerWinter: Summer can now leave a careful gift for winter.
messages.principle.summerWinterDone: Summer can now leave gifts for winter.
messages.season.springPreview: Spring preview · Dormant growth resumes, seed allowances renew and suitable wildlife may return.
messages.season.summerPreview: Summer preview · Water storage and mulch become most valuable while fresh cherries can be harvested and shared.
messages.season.winterPreview: Winter preview · Soil cover and shelter still shape what survives, even when no young crops are present.
messages.season.springSeedSwap: Spring sowing — your seed bank filled the swap table with free seedlings
messages.challenge.turnInstruction: Turn the season and let the lesson change your garden state.
messages.summary.bareDecision: You paused to observe before filling the empty plot.
messages.summary.guildReflection: You looked between the elements — that is where my strongest design lives.
messages.summary.pauseReflection: You paused before acting. That small pause is one of the best tools you can bring me.
messages.summary.systemsReflection: You practised decisions that account for several parts of the system at once.
messages.summary.connectionReflection: You practised reading a design connection as an exchange of needs and yields, not a collection of objects.
messages.summary.mulchReflection: You read my driest places first. Now sunlight can reach the leaves without taking so much from the soil.
messages.summary.mulchReflectionAlt: You read my driest places first. Now the sun reaches the leaves without stealing so much from the soil.
messages.summary.predatorReflection: You did not silence every insect. You rebuilt the conversation between them.
messages.summary.allLayers: 🌻 Every learning layer is represented — now watch how the real garden responds.
messages.summary.allThemes: 🏆 Every learning theme is represented. A real garden remains an ongoing practice of observation and care.
messages.challenge.voice.mulch: My driest places came first. Now the sun can reach the leaves without taking so much from the soil.
messages.challenge.voice.compost: Yesterday's scraps are warming. Nothing disappeared; only their work changed.
messages.challenge.voice.hugel: Wood that once fell can help rain linger beneath new roots. Watch what the mound does when the dry days come.
messages.challenge.voice.rain: The next rain will pause, fill the tank, overflow safely, and sink in — instead of hurrying away.
messages.challenge.voice.kitchen: Summer can leave gifts for winter now.
messages.challenge.voice.ladybug: Not every insect had to fall silent. Instead, the conversation between the garden's inhabitants returned.
messages.challenge.voice.bee: One season of flowers now passes its work to the next.
messages.challenge.voice.shelter: Even while I sleep, I am not empty. Safe shelter remains here for the quiet season.
messages.challenge.voice.pexeso: Now you see what lives between the elements. That is where the strength of my design is found.
messages.challenge.voice.seeds: Tomorrow's garden is already held in a handful of carefully chosen seeds.
messages.challenge.voice.quiz: Before action came a short pause. It is one of the best tools you can bring me.
